1. Common Language: Antigen vs Antibody

Why this lectureDr. Boita (clinical supplement to the viral hepatitis brick) focuses on hepatitis B because it is highly tested: it forces you to separate antigen from antibody, IgM from IgG, and to interpret serology. The ScholarRx brick sections are marked Brick.
  • Antigen = a substance recognized by the immune system; here a viral protein (HBsAg, HBcAg, HBeAg).
  • Antibody (immunoglobulin) = produced by the host in response to the antigen.
  • IgM comes first (acute or recent infection); IgG comes second (later; past infection or immunity). This is a general rule of immunology.
Antigen vs antibody; IgM vs IgG (slide 2) (click to enlarge)
HBV componentWhat it is
HBsAgSurface antigen (envelope)
HBcAgCore antigen (nucleocapsid, inside the virus)
HBeAgE antigen: marks replication (infectious)

2. Hepatitis B Work-up: Serology and the Window Period

ScenarioA patient has elevated AST/ALT. One cause is hepatitis, so you check for viral hepatitis, especially HBV, which can become dangerous.

The three tests ordered

TestQuestion it answers
HBsAg (surface antigen)Is the virus present? Positive = current infection
Anti-HBs (surface antibody)Immunity or susceptibility
Total anti-HBc (core antibody)Exposure to the actual virus; resolves the window period and tells infection from vaccine
HBV lab work-up flowchart (slide 3) (click to enlarge)

HBsAg positive: current infection

  • Order anti-HBc IgM and IgG. IgM = newly infected/acute; IgG = often chronic. (You can have both positive in early infection.)
  • If anti-HBc IgG is positive (chronic pattern), decide whether the virus is replicating:
    • HBeAg positive = infectious / increased viral replication (more spread, more hepatocellular damage).
    • Anti-HBe positive (seroconversion; HBeAg negative) = carrier or decreased viral replication.

HBsAg negative: no active infection

  • Check anti-HBs:
    • Anti-HBs negative = susceptible or in the window period.
    • Anti-HBs positive = immune. Then use anti-HBc: total anti-HBc positive = recovered natural infection; anti-HBc negative = vaccinated (vaccine gives only surface antibody).
  • Employers typically ask whether you are immune or susceptible (anti-HBs).

Interpretation table

PatternHBsAgAnti-HBsAnti-HBcMeaning
Current infection+−IgM + (acute) / IgG + (chronic)Infected; check HBeAg for replication
Recovered natural infection−++Immune from infection
Vaccinated−+−Immune from vaccine
Susceptible−−−Never infected or vaccinated
Window period−−+ (IgM / total)Recent infection, not yet immune

The window period (often tested)

  • HBsAg has cleared (negative) but anti-HBs has not yet appeared (negative), so it looks like "never infected and not immune."
  • That is why you order total anti-HBc: it is positive and reveals a recent infection.
HBV serology over time with window period (slide 4) (click to enlarge)
  • Graph: HBsAg and HBeAg rise first; symptoms and ↑ALT around months 2-4; anti-HBc IgM rises early then falls; anti-HBc IgG stays; HBsAg is mostly gone by ~month 6 before anti-HBs IgG appears (the window); anti-HBe rises as HBeAg falls.

Why it matters clinically

  • Chronic HBV is strongly linked to hepatocellular carcinoma (hepatocytes dividing and being injured repeatedly).
  • Active replication (HBeAg+) means more ongoing damage.
  • Most medications are metabolized in the liver and cleared by the kidney; starting a hepatically processed or hepatotoxic drug in someone in the window period (thought to be fine) could push them into liver failure.

Anti-HBe is non-protective. HBeAg positive = still contagious.

3. The Five Hepatitis Viruses: High-Yield Table and Brick Supplement

VirusGenome / envelopeKey antigensTransmissionStep 1 tips
HAVssRNA, non-envelopedCapsid proteinsFecal-oral (food/water): travel and shellfishUsually acute, self-limited; vaccine
HBVdsDNA, envelopedHBsAg, HBcAg, HBeAg (replication)Blood, sex, vertical (perinatal)Chronic in ~10%; serology-driven diagnosis; vaccine; → HCC
HCVssRNA, envelopedCore, E1/E2Blood (IV drug use, transfusion), less often sexOften chronic; no vaccine; major cause of cirrhosis and HCC
HDVssRNA, circular, enveloped via HBVDelta antigen (needs HBsAg)Blood, sex (like HBV)Only with HBV; coinfection vs superinfection; "viroid-like"
HEVssRNA, non-envelopedCapsid proteinsFecal-oral (water)Usually acute; severe in pregnancy; no widely used vaccine
Hepatitis virus table (slide 5) (click to enlarge)

Lecture points by virus

  • HAV: traveler to a developing country or shellfish eater with hepatitis; self-limited; vaccine.
  • HBV: the only dsDNA hepatitis virus; transmitted by blood, sex, vertical. Vertical transmission has a higher rate of chronicity; overall about 10% become chronic. Vaccine is among the first given to newborns before leaving the hospital.
  • HCV: blood, IV drug use; much higher chronicity, so cirrhosis and HCC (cirrhosis of any cause raises HCC risk); no vaccine because it replicates and mutates quickly.
  • HDV: cannot replicate on its own; needs HBV; blood and sex. A patient with chronic stable HBV who suddenly becomes severely decompensated or has fulminant hepatitis suggests HDV superinfection.
  • HEV: fecal-oral; perinatal transmission possible; severe fulminant hepatitis, especially in pregnancy.
Brick: structureHAV Picornaviridae, +ssRNA, non-enveloped. HBV Hepadnaviridae, dsDNA, enveloped. HCV Flaviviridae, +ssRNA, enveloped. HDV Deltavirus, -ssRNA virusoid with an HBsAg envelope; seen in the US mostly in IV drug users. HEV Hepeviridae, +ssRNA, non-enveloped. "Hepatitis virus" is not a taxonomic category.

Brick: replication, HBV vs HCV

HBVHCV
AttachmentNTCP (sodium taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide), almost only on hepatocytesApolipoprotein E (a liver-specific surface receptor, per the brick)
Genome stepCapsid enters the nucleus; dsDNA repaired to cccDNA; host RNA polymerase makes mRNA; some mRNA is reverse transcribedStays in the cytoplasm; +ssRNA makes proteins and a -ssRNA template via RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Key consequenceReverse transcription (reverse transcriptase function)RdRp is error-prone → high mutation rate ("quasi-species") → no vaccine
ReleaseAssembly in ER, exocytosis with membrane envelopeAssembly, exocytosis with membrane envelope

Brick: serology of the other viruses

VirusTestsInterpretation
HAVAnti-HAV IgM / IgGIgM = acute; IgG = past exposure, vaccination or end of infection. Rarely done (self-limited)
HCVAnti-HCV IgG and HCV RNA (PCR)RNA positive = active infection; anti-HCV positive = exposed at some point. RNA positive within 2-3 weeks; antibody 2-3 months. Test ~4 weeks after exposure
HDVAnti-HDV IgGUsed in new HBV diagnosis, or chronic HBV with acutely worsening liver function
HEVAnti-HEV IgM / IgGIgM = recent; IgG = clearing or prior exposure. Not typically used in the US
  • Viral load by PCR (HCV RNA, HBV DNA) is especially useful for response to therapy.

4. Most Common Causes of Hepatitis and How to Tell Them Apart

  • Worldwide the most common cause of hepatitis is viral; in the US it is alcohol use disorder (alcoholic hepatitis), with MASH/NASH also very common.
  • Most liver toxins can cause hepatitis: acetaminophen, antibiotics, valproic acid, chemotherapy agents, kava, anabolic steroids.
Differential of hepatitis (slide 6) (click to enlarge)
AlcoholicViralMetabolic (MASH, Wilson, hemochromatosis, A1AT)Autoimmune
CauseChronic ethanol → acetaldehyde and ROS toxicityHepatitis A-E (esp. B, C)Metabolic or geneticT-cell attack on hepatocytes (loss of tolerance)
Mechanism↑NADH/NAD+ → fat; Kupffer activation → stellate fibrosisDirect cytotoxicity and immune-mediated lysisLipid, copper or iron accumulation → oxidative stressAutoantibodies, chronic inflammation
HistologyMallory-Denk bodies, ballooned hepatocytes, neutrophils, zone 3 fibrosisLymphocytes, Councilman bodies, interface hepatitisSteatosis; copper or iron; PAS+ globules (A1AT)Plasma cells, interface hepatitis, rosettes
LabsAST > ALT (2:1), ↑GGT, ↑bilirubinALT > AST, often >1000↑ferritin (hemochromatosis); ↓ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings (Wilson); ↑TG (MASH)Very high transaminases, ↑IgG; type 1: ANA/SMA; type 2: LKM
CluesAlcohol history, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, gynecomastiaViral exposure, fatigue, jaundice, arthralgiaObesity, diabetes, family historyYoung-middle-aged woman, other autoimmune disease
TreatmentAbstinence, nutrition, steroids (severe)Antivirals (B and C); supportive (A and E)Treat the underlying causeImmunosuppression (steroids ± azathioprine)
Why finding the cause mattersImmunosuppressants treat autoimmune hepatitis but can worsen a viral cause. Autoimmune diseases tend to cluster (e.g. hypothyroidism, Sjogren).
  • AST:ALT: alcoholic hepatitis AST > ALT (2:1); viral hepatitis is the opposite (ALT > AST).
  • Mallory-Denk bodies: be able to recognize them from a description (they appear in the alcohol brick; boards-fair-game).
  • Jaundice pattern: if hepatocytes are destroyed and cannot conjugate, unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises; with biliary obstruction, conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood. This helps localize the problem (in the liver vs after the liver).
